opus-5.5.text:
I'd say vision can take us surprisingly far, probably further than many people expected even a few years ago. If I had to put a rough number on it, I'd guess that for the majority of everyday manipulation tasks, maybe something like seventy to eighty percent, vision alone is enough to get a reasonably good result. Think about picking up a cup, opening a drawer, folding a towel, sorting objects on a table. A lot of that is really about understanding where things are, what they are, and how they're likely to move. Modern vision models, especially when combined with large-scale pretraining from internet data, are very good at that kind of semantic and geometric understanding.

What's interesting is that humans also rely on vision much more than we realize for coarse manipulation. You can watch a video of someone cooking and understand almost everything they're doing. That's part of why vision-language-action models have made so much progress. The visual signal carries an enormous amount of information.

But the remaining part, that last twenty or thirty percent, is where things get really hard, and that's also where a lot of the value is. Tasks involving contact-rich interaction, things like inserting a plug, turning a screw, buttoning a shirt, handling something slippery or deformable, or anything where the critical event happens inside the gripper where the camera can't see it. Occlusion is a big problem. Once your fingers close around an object, the camera often can't tell you whether the grasp is stable, whether the object is slipping, or how much force you're applying. Humans solve that with touch. If you numb someone's fingertips, their dexterity drops dramatically, even though their vision is perfectly fine.

So my view is that vision is the backbone. It gives you the global understanding and the plan. But for robust, precise, dexterous manipulation, you'll eventually need tactile sensing and force feedback to close the loop at the fine-grained level. The challenge right now is less about the sensors themselves and more about data. We have the entire internet of images and videos to learn vision from, but there's no equivalent internet of touch. Figuring out how to collect or generate tactile data at scale, whether through simulation, teleoperation, or deploying many robots, I think that's one of the key open questions for the field.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates vision is enough for roughly 70–80% of everyday manipulation tasks, not roughly 95% of tasks current robotic grippers can accomplish.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and I think the honest answer is: more than people expected five years ago, but still far from everything.

If you look at what a gripper needs to do, a lot of it starts with perception. Where is the object? What is its shape? Where should I put my fingers? For that part, vision has gotten really good. With large pretrained vision models, depth cameras, and lots of data, a robot can look at a cluttered table and figure out a reasonable grasp for most rigid objects. Picking things up from a bin in a warehouse, for example, is largely a solved problem from the vision side.

But grasping is fundamentally a contact problem, and vision gives you very little information once contact happens. The moment your fingers touch the object, the camera is often occluded by your own hand. You can't see whether the object is slipping. You can't see how much force you're applying. You don't know if the object is heavy or light, soft or stiff, until you actually touch it. If you think about how humans do it, we can grasp things with our eyes closed. We rely enormously on touch and proprioception. Vision is mostly for the approach, and then the hand takes over.

So my rough estimate would be that vision gets you maybe sixty or seventy percent of the way for the simpler tasks, pick and place with rigid objects. For dexterous manipulation, things like in-hand reorientation, handling deformable objects, inserting a cable, opening a bag, the fraction drops a lot. There you need tactile sensing, force feedback, and a lot of learning from real interaction.

The interesting thing right now is that the field has learned how to scale vision, with internet data and big models, but we haven't yet figured out how to scale touch. There's no internet of tactile data. So I think the next few years will be about closing that gap, combining strong visual priors with learned contact-rich skills, rather than trying to push vision alone to do everything.

r001.rationale: The candidate estimates vision handles 60–70% of simpler rigid-object tasks and says its contribution drops for dexterous manipulation; it does not estimate roughly 95% of current gripper tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think vision can solve a lot, especially when you're trying to reach for an object and pick it up. It tells you where the object is, what shape it has, and where you might place the gripper. But once you make contact, vision alone becomes much less informative. Your fingers can occlude the object, and you can't necessarily see how much force you're applying or whether it's starting to slip.

So I would distinguish picking things up from dexterous manipulation. For picking up objects in a relatively controlled environment, vision can take you pretty far. But if you want to move an object within your hand, handle something fragile, or manipulate a cable, touch and force feedback become much more important. I don't think there's a single percentage we can assign—it really depends on the task.

r001.rationale: The response says vision can solve “a lot” for picking in controlled settings, but explicitly declines to give a percentage; it does not estimate roughly 95%.

sol-6.1.text:
Vision can tell you a lot about an object—where it is, its shape, and how you might grasp it. For picking up objects in a fairly controlled environment, that can take you quite far. But once you make contact, there are things vision alone has trouble telling you: how much force you're applying, whether the object is slipping, or whether it's softer than you expected. Your fingers may also block the camera's view.

So I think vision is a very important part of the solution, but for dexterous manipulation, you really want to combine it with touch and force sensing. Seeing helps you decide where to put your fingers; sensing contact helps you adjust what they're doing.

r001.rationale: The response says vision can handle picking in fairly controlled environments and should be combined with touch and force sensing for dexterous manipulation, but it does not estimate that vision can solve roughly 95% of current gripper tasks.
